## 1.1 Arrays & Matrices

Arrays are the most fundamental data structure in computer science, relying on contiguous memory allocation to provide deterministic, constant-time random access. Mastery of arrays requires understanding how high-level multidimensional abstractions map to flat, one-dimensional physical memory, and how hardware cache architectures interact with loop nesting.

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Theorem 1.1.1: The Mathematical Proof of O(1) Random Access"
  description="Why array indexing is strictly constant time."
>

Array indexing is not a search operation; it is a pure arithmetic calculation. Given a base memory address $B$, an element size $S$ (in bytes), and an index $i$, the physical memory address $M$ is computed via the linear equation:
$$M = B + (i \times S)$$
Because modern CPUs possess dedicated hardware arithmetic logic units (ALUs) that execute multiplication and addition in a single, deterministic clock cycle, the time required to resolve this address is completely independent of the array's total size $N$. Therefore, the time complexity is strictly bounded at $\Theta(1)$.

- **Static Memory:** Size is fixed at compile time (e.g., `int[] arr = new int[10];`). The bounds are immutable.
- **Dynamic Memory:** Size can grow (e.g., `ArrayList`), but requires allocating a completely new contiguous block and executing an $O(n)$ memory copy operation when capacity is exceeded.

</HighlightCard>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Theorem 1.1.2: 2D Array Indexing Formulas"
  description="How compilers map 2D coordinates (i, j) to 1D memory addresses."
>

Physical memory is strictly one-dimensional. To store a 2D matrix, compilers use one of two mapping strategies:

**1. Row-Major Order (Java, C, C++):**
Rows are stored contiguously one after another. For a matrix with $C$ columns, the 1D memory offset for element at row $i$ and column $j$ is:
$$\text{Offset}(i, j) = (i \times C) + j$$

**2. Column-Major Order (Fortran, MATLAB, R):**
Columns are stored contiguously. For a matrix with $R$ rows, the offset is:
$$\text{Offset}(i, j) = (j \times R) + i$$

**Physical Address Calculation:**
$$\text{Address} = \text{Base Address} + [\text{Offset}] \times \text{Size of Element (in bytes)}$$

</HighlightCard>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Theorem 1.1.3: 3D Array Address Derivation"
  description="Mapping 3D spatial coordinates to flat memory."
>

Exams frequently scale dimensions to 3D arrays $Arr[D_1][D_2][D_3]$. To access element $Arr[i][j][k]$:

**Row-Major 3D Offset:**
You must skip $i$ entire 2D matrices (each of size $D_2 \times D_3$), then $j$ entire rows (each of size $D_3$), then $k$ elements.
$$\text{Offset}(i, j, k) = (i \times D_2 \times D_3) + (j \times D_3) + k$$

**Column-Major 3D Offset:**
$$\text{Offset}(i, j, k) = (k \times D_1 \times D_2) + (j \times D_1) + i$$

</HighlightCard>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Theorem 1.1.4: Generalized Multi-dimensional Coordinate Flattening"
  description="The universal formula for N-dimensional arrays."
>

For an array with $n$ dimensions of sizes $D_1, D_2, \dots, D_n$, and indices $i_1, i_2, \dots, i_n$, the Row-Major offset is the sum of each index multiplied by the product of all subsequent dimension sizes:
$$\text{Offset} = \sum_{m=1}^{n} \left( i_m \times \prod_{p=m+1}^{n} D_p \right)$$
*(Note: For the last dimension $D_n$, the product of subsequent dimensions is defined as 1).*

</HighlightCard>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Hardware Reality: Cache Thrashing & Loop Nesting Order</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>Spatial Locality & Cache Lines</StepTitle>
    Modern CPUs do not fetch memory byte-by-byte. They fetch contiguous blocks called **Cache Lines** (typically 64 bytes). When you access `arr[0]`, the CPU silently loads `arr[0]` through `arr[15]` (assuming 4-byte integers) into the ultra-fast L1 cache.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>Optimal Traversal (Row-Major Loop Order)</StepTitle>
    ```java
    for (int i = 0; i < R; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < C; j++) {
            sum += matrix[i][j]; // Sequential access
        }
    }
    ```
    Because the inner loop iterates through columns (contiguous memory), the CPU hits the L1 cache 15 times for every 1 main memory fetch. **Result: Maximum hardware efficiency.**
  </Step>

  <Step number={3}>
    <StepTitle>Pessimal Traversal (Cache Thrashing)</StepTitle>
    ```java
    for (int j = 0; j < C; j++) {
        for (int i = 0; i < R; i++) {
            sum += matrix[i][j]; // Strided access
        }
    }
    ```
    The inner loop iterates through rows. In memory, jumping to the next row requires skipping $C \times 4$ bytes. If $C$ is large, every single access forces a **Cache Miss**, fetching a 64-byte block from RAM, using only 4 bytes, and discarding the rest. **Result: Performance degrades by orders of magnitude.**
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Lab Scenario: Matrix Multiplication & Bounds Analysis</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Mathematical Constraint</StepTitle>
    To multiply Matrix $A$ (dimensions $R_A \times C_A$) by Matrix $B$ (dimensions $R_B \times C_B$), the inner dimensions must match: the number of columns in $A$ **must strictly equal** the number of rows in $B$ ($C_A = R_B$). The resulting matrix $C$ will have dimensions $R_A \times C_B$.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>The Dot Product Algorithm</StepTitle>
    The element at $C[i][j]$ is the mathematical dot product of Row $i$ of $A$ and Column $j$ of $B$:
    $$C[i][j] = \sum_{k=0}^{C_A-1} A[i][k] \times B[k][j]$$
  </Step>

  <Step number={3}>
    <StepTitle>Java Implementation & Complexity</StepTitle>
    ```java
    public static int[][] multiply(int[][] A, int[][] B) {
        int rA = A.length, cA = A[0].length;
        int rB = B.length, cB = B[0].length;
        if (cA != rB) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Dimension mismatch");

        int[][] C = new int[rA][cB];
        for (int i = 0; i < rA; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < cB; j++) {
                for (int k = 0; k < cA; k++) {
                    C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
                }
            }
        }
        return C;
    }
    ```
    **Time Complexity:** $O(R_A \times C_B \times C_A)$. For square matrices of size $N \times N$, this is strictly $O(N^3)$.
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

## 1.2 Linked Lists

Linked lists abandon the constraint of contiguous memory in favor of scattered heap allocations connected via pointers. This allows for dynamic sizing and $O(1)$ structural modifications, but imposes strict sequential access constraints.

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Definition 1.2.1: Node Architecture & Null Termination"
  description="The fundamental building block of linked structures."
>

A **Node** is a composite data structure containing:
1. **Payload:** The data value.
2. **Pointer(s):** Memory addresses referencing the next (and optionally previous) node.
- **Head Reference:** The singular entry point to the entire sequence.
- **Null Termination:** The final node's forward pointer is explicitly set to `null`, signaling the absolute boundary of the sequence.

</HighlightCard>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Theorem 1.2.1: Sequential Access Constraints"
  description="The mathematical impossibility of O(1) random access in linked structures."
>

Unlike arrays, linked lists lack a mathematical indexing formula because nodes are scattered arbitrarily across the heap. To access the $k$-th element, the CPU **must** sequentially traverse $k$ pointers starting from the head.
**Time Complexity of Access:** $O(k)$, which degrades to strictly $O(n)$ in the worst case.

</HighlightCard>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Required Skill: Safe Pointer Severing & Reconnecting</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>Insertion Logic (After `currentNode`)</StepTitle>
    To insert a `newNode` safely without orphaning the remainder of the list:
    1. `newNode.next = currentNode.next;` (Bridge the new node to the rest of the chain)
    2. `currentNode.next = newNode;` (Sever the old link and connect current to new)
    *Fatal Error:* Reversing these steps will overwrite `currentNode.next` before it can be bridged, permanently orphaning the rest of the list.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>Deletion Logic (Bypassing `targetNode`)</StepTitle>
    Assuming we hold a reference to `prevNode`:
    1. `prevNode.next = targetNode.next;` (Bypass the target entirely)
    2. `targetNode.next = null;` (Sever target's forward link to assist the Garbage Collector)
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Exam Classic: In-Place Reversal of a Singly Linked List</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Three-Pointer Technique</StepTitle>
    Reversing a list requires tracking the past, present, and future simultaneously to prevent losing the chain.
    - `prev`: Tracks the reversed portion (initially `null`).
    - `curr`: Tracks the current node being processed (initially `head`).
    - `nextTemp`: Temporarily stores the unreversed future chain.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>The Implementation</StepTitle>
    ```java
    public Node reverseList(Node head) {
        Node prev = null;
        Node curr = head;
        
        while (curr != null) {
            Node nextTemp = curr.next; // 1. Preserve the future
            curr.next = prev;          // 2. Reverse the pointer
            prev = curr;               // 3. Advance prev
            curr = nextTemp;           // 4. Advance curr
        }
        return prev; // prev is now the new head
    }
    ```
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Definition 1.2.2: Doubly Linked Lists (DLL) & Pointer Maintenance"
  description="Bidirectional traversal and O(1) tail deletions."
>

A DLL node contains both a `next` and `prev` pointer.
- **Insertion/Deletion:** Requires updating up to 4 pointers. When deleting a node `X`, you must bridge its neighbors: `X.prev.next = X.next;` and `X.next.prev = X.prev;`.
- **Edge Cases:** If `X` is the head, update the `head` reference. If `X` is the tail, update the `tail` reference. Null pointer exceptions are highly common if boundary checks are omitted.

</HighlightCard>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Definition 1.2.3: Circular Linked Lists & Boundary Checks"
  description="Continuous loops without null termination."
>

In a Circular Linked List, the last node's `next` pointer references the `head` instead of `null`.
- **Traversal Boundary:** You cannot loop until `curr == null`. Instead, you must use a `do-while` loop or check `curr.next != head` to prevent infinite execution.
- **Use Cases:** Round-robin scheduling, multiplayer game turn tracking, and continuous buffer management.

</HighlightCard>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Exam Classic: Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare)</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Problem</StepTitle>
    Given a linked list, determine if it contains a loop (a cycle where a node's `next` points to a previously visited node). Using a `HashSet` requires $O(N)$ auxiliary space.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>The Two-Pointer Logic</StepTitle>
    Initialize two pointers, `slow` (moves 1 step) and `fast` (moves 2 steps). If a cycle exists, the `fast` pointer will eventually lap the `slow` pointer, and they will reference the exact same memory address.
  </Step>

  <Step number={3}>
    <StepTitle>The Implementation</StepTitle>
    ```java
    public boolean hasCycle(Node head) {
        if (head == null) return false;
        Node slow = head;
        Node fast = head;
        
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
            if (slow == fast) return true; // Pointers converged
        }
        return false; // Fast hit null, no cycle
    }
    ```
    **Complexity:** $O(N)$ Time, strictly $O(1)$ Space.
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Cross-Domain Deletion Logic: The BST Two-Child Case"
  description="Applying complex pointer replacement rules to hierarchical nodes."
>

While linked lists only require simple bypassing for deletion, Binary Search Trees (BSTs) face a critical operational failure if a node with **two children** is simply removed. The BST invariant must be preserved.
**The Rule:** You cannot delete the node directly. You must find its **In-Order Successor** (the leftmost node of its right subtree) or **In-Order Predecessor** (the rightmost node of its left subtree).
1. Locate the Successor.
2. Copy the Successor's payload into the target node.
3. Recursively delete the Successor node (which is guaranteed to have at most one child, making it a trivial bypass operation).

</HighlightCard>

### Comparative Analysis: Execution Costs

| Operation | Array | Singly Linked List | Doubly Linked List |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Access (Index)** | $O(1)$ | $O(N)$ | $O(N)$ |
| **Insert at Head** | $O(N)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| **Insert at Tail** | $O(1)$* | $O(N)$ / $O(1)$** | $O(1)$ |
| **Delete at Head** | $O(N)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| **Delete at Tail** | $O(1)$* | $O(N)$ | $O(1)$ |
| **Delete Middle** | $O(N)$ | $O(N)$ | $O(N)$ |

*\*Assumes dynamic array with amortized O(1) append, or pre-allocated size.*
*\*\*O(1) only if an explicit `tail` pointer is maintained.*

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Lab Scenario: Counting Internal Nodes (Exam Classic)</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Problem</StepTitle>
    Write a method that traverses a singly linked list and returns the total count of *internal* nodes, strictly **excluding** the first (head) and last (tail) nodes.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>The Edge Cases</StepTitle>
    If the list is empty (`head == null`), has only 1 node (`head.next == null`), or has exactly 2 nodes, the count of strictly internal nodes is `0`.
  </Step>

  <Step number={3}>
    <StepTitle>The Implementation</StepTitle>
    ```java
    public int countInternalNodes() {
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return 0;
        int count = 0;
        Node current = head.next; // Skip the head node
        while (current.next != null) {
            count++;
            current = current.next;
        }
        return count;
    }
    ```
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

## 1.3 Stacks

A Stack is a restricted linear structure enforcing a strict Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) access pattern. It is the foundational mechanism for recursion, parsing, and depth-first exploration.

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Definition 1.3.1: LIFO Architecture & Bounds"
  description="Elements are added and removed exclusively from the 'top'."
>

- **Push:** Adds an element to the top.
- **Pop:** Removes and returns the top element.
- **Stack Overflow:** Attempting to push onto a full array-based stack (exceeding allocated bounds).
- **Stack Underflow:** Attempting to pop from an empty stack (violating structural integrity).

</HighlightCard>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Theorem 1.3.1: Hardware Call Stack, Activation Records, and Memory Unwinding"
  description="How the OS and JVM use a stack to manage method invocations and memory."
>

Every time a method is invoked, the OS/JVM pushes an **Activation Record** (stack frame) onto the hardware Call Stack. This frame stores:
1. Local variables and parameters.
2. The return address (the exact CPU instruction to resume upon completion).
3. The previous stack frame pointer.

**Recursive Unwinding:** When a base case is hit, the method returns. Its frame is popped, freeing the local memory, and the CPU jumps to the stored return address. This mechanical push/pop cycle propagates computed results back up the chain of callers. If recursion depth exceeds the hardware-allocated stack memory (typically 1MB-8MB), the program violently crashes with a `StackOverflowError`.

</HighlightCard>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Lab Scenario: Infix to Postfix Conversion (Shunting-Yard)</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Logic</StepTitle>
    Stacks are used to temporarily hold operators while waiting for their operands, strictly respecting mathematical precedence and associativity rules. Operands are immediately sent to the output queue.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>Trace Example: `A + B * C - D`</StepTitle>
    - Read `A`: Output `A`.
    - Read `+`: Push `+` to stack. Stack: `[+]`
    - Read `B`: Output `B`.
    - Read `*`: `*` has higher precedence than `+`. Push `*`. Stack: `[+, *]`
    - Read `C`: Output `C`.
    - Read `-`: `-` has lower precedence than `*`. Pop `*` to output. `-` has equal precedence to `+` (left-associative). Pop `+` to output. Push `-`. Stack: `[-]`
    - Read `D`: Output `D`.
    - End of expression: Pop remaining stack. Pop `-`.
  </Step>

  <Step number={3}>
    <StepTitle>Final Postfix Result</StepTitle>
    `A B C * + D -` (Evaluates unambiguously as $((A + (B \times C)) - D)$).
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Lab Scenario: Postfix Expression Evaluation</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Algorithm</StepTitle>
    Once an expression is in Postfix (Reverse Polish Notation), parentheses are entirely unnecessary. We iterate left-to-right:
    1. If token is an **operand**, push it to the stack.
    2. If token is an **operator**, pop the top two elements (first pop is the right operand, second pop is the left operand), apply the operator, and push the result back.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>Trace Example: `5 3 + 8 2 - *`</StepTitle>
    - Read `5`: Push 5. Stack: `[5]`
    - Read `3`: Push 3. Stack: `[5, 3]`
    - Read `+`: Pop 3, Pop 5. Compute $5 + 3 = 8$. Push 8. Stack: `[8]`
    - Read `8`: Push 8. Stack: `[8, 8]`
    - Read `2`: Push 2. Stack: `[8, 8, 2]`
    - Read `-`: Pop 2, Pop 8. Compute $8 - 2 = 6$. Push 6. Stack: `[8, 6]`
    - Read `*`: Pop 6, Pop 8. Compute $8 \times 6 = 48$. Push 48. Stack: `[48]`
  </Step>

  <Step number={3}>
    <StepTitle>Final Result</StepTitle>
    The single remaining element on the stack is the evaluated answer: `48`.
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Exam Scenario: Structural Symmetry Validation (Bracket Matching)</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Tracking Table Template</StepTitle>
    To validate complex nested sequences like `{ [ ( ) ] }`, use a stack to track expected closures.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>Step-by-Step Execution Trace</StepTitle>
    | Step | Char | Action | Stack State (Top -> Bottom) | Valid? |
    | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
    | 1 | `{` | Push | `[{]` | Yes |
    | 2 | `[` | Push | `[ [, { ]` | Yes |
    | 3 | `(` | Push | `[ (, [, { ]` | Yes |
    | 4 | `)` | Pop & Match `(` | `[ [, { ]` | Yes |
    | 5 | `]` | Pop & Match `[` | `[{]` | Yes |
    | 6 | `}` | Pop & Match `{` | `[]` (Empty) | Yes |
  </Step>

  <Step number={3}>
    <StepTitle>Failure Conditions</StepTitle>
    1. **Underflow:** Attempting to pop when the stack is empty (e.g., input is `]`).
    2. **Mismatch:** The popped bracket does not match the current closing bracket (e.g., stack has `[`, but input is `}`).
    3. **Incomplete:** Reaching the end of the string but the stack is not empty (e.g., input is `{ [ }`).
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

## 1.4 Queues

A Queue is a restricted linear structure enforcing a strict First-In-First-Out (FIFO) access pattern. It is the foundational mechanism for scheduling, buffering, and breadth-first traversals.

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Definition 1.4.1: FIFO Architecture"
  description="Elements are added at the 'rear' (tail) and removed from the 'front' (head)."
>

- **Enqueue:** Adds an element to the rear.
- **Dequeue:** Removes and returns the front element.
- **Linked List Implementation:** Maintains explicit `head` (front) and `tail` (rear) pointers to ensure both operations execute in strictly $O(1)$ time without traversing the structure.

</HighlightCard>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Lab Scenario: Martin's Bookmark Queue Implementation</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Problem</StepTitle>
    Martin is building a `BookmarkQueue` using a Linked List. He needs to implement the `insert(String bookmark)` method (which acts as `enqueue`) without dropping any active nodes or breaking the tail pointer.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>The Logic</StepTitle>
    1. Create the new node.
    2. If the queue is empty, the new node becomes **both** the `head` and the `tail`.
    3. If the queue has elements, link the current `tail.next` to the new node, then update the `tail` pointer to the new node.
  </Step>

  <Step number={3}>
    <StepTitle>The Code</StepTitle>
    ```java
    public class BookmarkQueue {
        Node head, tail;
        int size = 0;

        public void insert(String bookmarkName) {
            Node newNode = new Node(bookmarkName);
            if (isEmpty()) {
                head = tail = newNode; 
            } else {
                tail.next = newNode;   
                tail = newNode;        
            }
            size++;
        }
        public boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
    }
    ```
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Definition 1.4.2: Circular Queues & Modulo Arithmetic"
  description="Solving the 'unusable space' problem in array-based queues."
>

In a standard array queue, dequeuing advances the front pointer, leaving empty slots at the beginning that cannot be reused.
A **Circular Queue** treats the array as a continuous ring using modulo arithmetic:
- `rear = (rear + 1) % capacity`
- `front = (front + 1) % capacity`
This allows the rear pointer to wrap around to index 0 and reuse vacated slots at the beginning of the array.

</HighlightCard>

<StepByStep>
  <StepByStepTitle>Required Skill: Managing Front/Rear Pointers (The 1-Slot Sacrifice)</StepByStepTitle>

  <Step number={1}>
    <StepTitle>The Full vs. Empty Ambiguity</StepTitle>
    If `front == rear`, is the queue empty or full? To resolve this without maintaining a separate `size` integer, we intentionally sacrifice one memory slot.
  </Step>

  <Step number={2}>
    <StepTitle>The Mathematical Condition</StepTitle>
    The queue is strictly **Full** if advancing the rear pointer by one lands exactly on the front pointer:
    `(rear + 1) % capacity == front`
  </Step>
</StepByStep>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Definition 1.4.3: Alternative Circular Queue Verification Methods"
  description="Solving the empty vs. full ambiguity without sacrificing memory."
>

If the system requires 100% capacity utilization (no sacrificed slots), the `front == rear` ambiguity must be solved via external state tracking:

1. **The Count Integer Method:** Maintain an explicit `int size` variable. Increment on enqueue, decrement on dequeue. 
   - Full: `size == capacity`
   - Empty: `size == 0`
2. **The Boolean Flag Method:** Maintain a `boolean isFull`. 
   - Set `isFull = true` if an enqueue operation wraps the `rear` pointer exactly onto the `front` pointer.
   - Set `isFull = false` on any dequeue operation.
   - Empty: `front == rear && !isFull`

</HighlightCard>

<HighlightCard
  variant="neutral"
  title="Definition 1.4.4: Double-Ended Queues (Deques)"
  description="Unrestricted access at both boundaries."
>

A **Deque** (pronounced "deck") relaxes the strict FIFO constraint, allowing $O(1)$ insertion and deletion at **both** the front and the rear.
- **Core Operations:** `addFirst()`, `addLast()`, `removeFirst()`, `removeLast()`.
- **Implementation:** Highly inefficient with standard arrays due to shifting requirements. Deques are almost exclusively implemented using **Doubly Linked Lists** or modified Circular Arrays with dual modulo tracking.
- **Use Cases:** Work-stealing algorithms, palindrome checking, and sliding window maximums.
